# 'killed' means a mutation taken from this sweep's output now fails a test.
# 'equivalent' means the mutation is real and the program is the same either way.

true as ConsumeRequestChunkedTEImmediately. AHTTPClient puts it on the request builder (298) and so on every request this client sends - and the only reader of a PDU's flag in the client is AHTTPClient 1346, which reads it on the *response*. On a request it is copied (HTTPRequest 1765) and never acted on: it decides how an incoming chunked body is read, and the client does not read its own request

EDNSOptions.Count > 0 ? EDNSOptions : null - [] and null make the same OPT record, see DNSClient 801. Here the query does reach the wire, and the octets are the same: an empty option list adds nothing to the RDLENGTH and writes nothing

soa.Minimum < soa.TimeToLive ? soa.Minimum : soa.TimeToLive, which is a minimum written as a conditional. RFC 2308 section 5 asks for exactly that: the negative answer's TTL 'is taken from the minimum of the SOA.MINIMUM field and SOA's TTL'. The mutant moves the comparison to <=, which changes only the case where the two fields are equal - and there both arms return the same value. A boundary on which the two programs compute the same number. CacheBoundaryTests checks the rule from both sides

Serialize(ms, UseCompression: false) for the UDP query. Since finding 86 a query carries exactly one question (the guard at 314 sends several types as several queries), and the only other name in it is the OPT record's owner, the root, which DNSServiceName.Serialize writes as a single zero octet before it ever looks at the offsets. With one name there is nothing a pointer could point at, so true and false write the same octets. A TSIG or SIG(0) record is appended after serialisation, by TransactionSecurity.SignQuery, and does not see the flag
entry.EndOfLife > Timestamp.Now in TryGetNoData

DomainName.IsNullOrEmpty() || DNSInformation is null, the guard on AddToCache. The four call sites (908, 937, 952, 1145) were read again: the name is either the query name, which the guard at the top of Query has already proved non-empty, or a parsed record's owner name, which is never null and is '.' at its shortest; and the response is non-null at each site by the condition that leads there. Both operands are false wherever this runs, so || and && do the same nothing
e.Expiry <= now, an NSEC range that has run out when a new one for the zone arrives. The line's other mutant, || to &&, is killed

received < 2 || ((data[0] << 8) | data[1]) != dnsQuery.TransactionId, the RFC 5452 section 4.2 pre-filter on an incoming datagram. Both of its mutants survive, and for one reason: the transaction id is checked twice and both checks react the same way. Whatever gets past this guard reaches DNSInfo.ReadResponse, which compares the id again and returns Invalid when it differs, and the caller answers `if (!response.IsValid) continue;` (476) - the `continue` this guard would have taken. || to && makes the pre-filter a no-op for any datagram of two octets or more, and < to <= moves only where a two-octet datagram is dropped. Neither changes what the client does or how long it waits. UdpDatagramAcceptanceTests asserts what both produce

EDNSOptions.Count > 0 ? EDNSOptions : null, building the query DNSClient hands on. [] and null make the same OPT record - OPT's constructor does `Options ?? []` (OPT.cs 183), and the record exists because UDPPayloadSize > 0 (DNSPacket 381), not because the list is non-null. Beyond that this query's options never reach the wire: QueryDNSServerAsync assigns effectiveQuery (1468), rebuilds it with the per-server cookie (1494) and never reads it again, and the transport takes the options from its own EDNSOptions
ForceUpdate = false, a parameter default - see DNSClient 1559
e.Expiry < now, the NSEC ranges it removes

nsecRecords.Count > 0, feeding the RFC 8198 denial cache. The block is guarded by firstResponse?.DNSSECStatus == DNSSECValidationResult.Secure, and DNSSECStatus is assigned nowhere in Hermod/DNS - it is a settable property the caller fills in after the fact, and the object read here was created inside this call. The comment above it says so: the path 'stays dormant. It is meant to'. Dead by design, so the mutant cannot be reached
EDNSOptions.Count > 0 ? EDNSOptions : null - see DNSUDPClient 336, the same line in the same shape

the `false` handed to transportClient.Query as its ForceUpdate. Grepped across the client folder at d906af2d: DNSClient.cs:682 is the only line that reads ForceUpdate. The transports declare the parameter and forward it, and none of them acts on it - they have no cache to bypass

remaining > TimeSpan.Zero ? remaining : TimeSpan.Zero, what is left of the query's deadline when the TCP retry starts, new in 38f6a355. The mutant moves the comparison to >=, which changes only the case where nothing is left - and there both arms are TimeSpan.Zero. The same number either way

disposedValue = true, the flag that makes Dispose idempotent. The body it guards already is: DNSCache.Dispose() is `cleanUpTimer.Dispose()` and a Timer tolerates being disposed twice, and transportClients is cleared on the first pass, so the second finds nothing. A second Dispose with the flag never set does the same nothing the flag prevents

new NetworkStream(socket, ownsSocket: false) in the TCP retry. With true the stream closes the socket when its `using` ends, at the end of the try block; the finally right after it (901) disposes the socket anyway, and Socket.Dispose is idempotent. The socket is closed a moment earlier, by the same call
Serialize(ms, UseCompression: false) for the TCP retry - the same query, see 360

disposedValue = true. The flag guards one call, lifetime.Cancel(), which is idempotent on a source that is never disposed - and `lifetime` is not. A second Dispose with the flag never set cancels a cancelled source again
Dispose(Disposing: true) from Dispose(). The parameter is read nowhere in Dispose(Boolean); true and false run the same body
